children.text: The telehealth reimbursement landscape for rural hospitals faces its most consequential policy moment since 2020. Unless Congress passes a permanent extension before December 31, 2026, the Medicare telehealth waivers that have governed rural hospital billing since the COVID-19 public health emergency will sunset, reverting to pre-pandemic restrictions that would disqualify the majority of services currently delivered via telehealth for Medicare reimbursement.
The Six Waivers at Risk and Their Financial Exposure

body.title: COVID-Era Telehealth Waivers Expiring December 31, 2026

children.text: The Legislative Outlook and Scenario Planning

As of early 2026, telehealth-extension bills — including the CONNECT for Health Act (permanent extension) and narrower two-year extensions — remain in play. The fiscal scoring of these bills is contested: CBO has scored short-term telehealth extensions in the range of a few billion dollars over two years, while CONNECT’s sponsors argue it would generate net savings. That disagreement over cost has repeatedly stalled permanent action despite bipartisan support.

The most likely legislative outcome, based on current committee dynamics, is a partial permanent extension covering rural originating site flexibility and audio-only services, with the home-as-originating-site and mental health waivers subject to a further two-year extension. Rural hospital revenue officers should model three scenarios: full extension, partial extension, and full expiration.

No rural hospital CFO should be operating without a telehealth waiver sunset contingency plan. The best-case legislative outcome still removes significant revenue. The worst case is an 8-figure exposure for mid-size rural systems.

CONTINGENCY PLANNING: Build three scenarios into FY 2027 budget: (1) Full Extension: revenue neutral; (2) Partial Extension (rural HPSA + audio-only): -$220K avg impact; (3) Full Sunset: -$840K avg impact. Begin renegotiating commercial payer telehealth rates NOW regardless of Medicare outcome—commercial rates are currently below cost in 62% of rural markets.

Renegotiate commercial payer telehealth rates—Medicare waiver sunset does not automatically affect commercial contracts
Join AHA rural advocacy coalition for CONNECT Act support—CBO scoring is the primary obstacle and rural hospital data is the most persuasive input

summary: The COVID-era telehealth flexibilities extended through December 31, 2026 under the Consolidated Appropriations Act will expire unless Congress acts. For rural hospitals that have built service line revenue on pandemic-era reimbursement rates, the expiration represents an average revenue exposure of $840,000 per facility. This analysis maps the specific waivers at risk, the reimbursement differential, and the legislative outlook.
title: The 2026 Telehealth Reimbursement Cliff: What Rural Hospitals Must Do Before the COVID-Era Waivers Expire V2
